'''''Hordeum murinum''''' is a [[species]] of [[flowering plant]] in the grass family [[Poaceae]], commonly known as '''wall barley''' or '''false barley'''. It is a close relative of [[Barley|cultivated barley]] (''H. vulgare'').

==Overview==
''Hordeum murinum'' complex is the most widespread and common of all ''Hordeum'' species.<ref name="Mizianty-2006" /> The center of distribution of ''H. murinum'' is in the Mediterranean area, Central Europe, Western Asia, and North Africa.<ref name="Mizianty-2006" /> It flowers during May through July in mainly coastal areas. It is an ancient introduction in the [[British Isles]], common in [[England]] and [[Wales]] but  less common in [[Scotland]] and [[Ireland]]. <ref name="Stroh">{{cite web |title=''Hordeum murinum'' L. |work=BSBI Online Plant Atlas 2020 |editor=P.A. Stroh |editor2=T. A. Humphrey |editor3=R.J. Burkmar |editor4=O.L. Pescott |editor5=D.B. Roy |editor6=K.J. Walker |url=https://plantatlas2020.org/atlas/2cd4p9h.c4e |publisher=[[Botanical Society of Britain and Ireland]]|access-date=10 June 2023 }}</ref>

It can grow to about  30-50 cm in height, and its unbranched spikes can reach 10 cm long. It produces small, dry seeds and its leaves can be {{Convert|8|mm|in|frac=64}} wide with short, blunt [[ligule]]s.
It is an annual species whose seeds germinate and develop in the spring.<ref name="Johnston-2009">{{Cite journal|url = https://apps.webofknowledge.com/full_record.do?product=UA&search_mode=GeneralSearch&qid=11&SID=4Cd9DHWv1Z42NyP4kld&page=1&doc=1&cacheurlFromRightClick=no|title=Effect of quality and distribution of rainfall of rainfalls on ''Hordeum murinum'' L. growth and development|last = Johnston|first = Myra|date = 2009|journal = Chilean Journal of Agricultural Research|doi = 10.4067/S0718-58392009000200008|doi-access = free}}</ref> ''Hordeum murinum'' ssp. ''murinum'' is also referred to as wall barley and is tetraploid.<ref name="Fleet-2012">

Among its subspecies is included [[#leporinum|''H. m.'' ssp. ''leporinum'']], known as '''hare barley'''.

==Growth requirements==
Precipitation is the most important factor in the production of seeds for this species. A greater quantity of dry material is produced with medium precipitation and better distribution.<ref name="Johnston-2009" /> In drier years with early or late rainfalls, there is no chance of re-seeding for this species.<ref name="Fleet-2012" /> The species uses a greater part of its reproductive resources for seed production, allowing it to adapt to different water conditions.<ref name="Johnston-2009" /> Controlling the seeding rate favors high-quality strands of barley. The sowing rate for wall barley increases when seed production and forage increases.<ref name="El-Shatnawi-2003">

The height of the plant and protein content does not respond to seeding rates, but the height of the plant and protein content does vary with years.<ref name="El-Shatnawi-2003" /> This weedy species along with hare barley and smooth barley can be hard to control.<ref name="Fleet-2012" />

==Subspecies==
There are three [[subspecies]]:

''Hordeum murinum'' ssp. ''{{Vanchor|leporinum}}'', known as '''hare barley''',<ref name="MMPND">{{Cite web | title = Sorting ''Hordeum'' names | work = Multilingual Multiscript Plant Name Database | url = http://www.plantnames.unimelb.edu.au/Sorting/Hordeum.html | access-date = 2009-01-06}}</ref> '''mouse barley''',<ref name="GRIN 102928">{{GRIN | name = ''Hordeum murinum'' subsp. ''leporinum'' (Link) Arcang. | id = 102928}}</ref> and '''barley grass'''.<ref name="FloraBase 449">{{FloraBase | name = ''Hordeum leporinum'' Link | id = 449}}</ref> This subspecies grows in tufts from {{cvt|10|to|40|cm|0}} in height,<ref name = "FloraBase 449"/><ref name="PlantNET">{{NSW Flora Online | genus = Hordeum | species = leporinum | author = Link}}</ref> and its flowers are attached to branches rather than to the main axis.{{CN|date=August 2023}} It is native to the Mediterranean region near continental, oceanic, and colder climates,<ref name="Mizianty-2006" /> as well as northern Africa and temperate Asia, and it is widely naturalised elsewhere.<ref name="GRIN 102928"/> It was first published as the full species ''H. leporinum'' by [[Johann Heinrich Friedrich Link]] in 1834. In 1882 it was redescribed as a subspecies of ''H. murinum'' by [[Giovanni Arcangeli]], though today some authorities maintain it at the species level.<ref name = "FloraBase 449"/><ref name="PlantNET"/> Jakob & Blattner 2009 find [[cytotype]]s of both [[tetraploid]] and [[hexaploid]].<ref name="Formation"/>

Another subspecies is ''Hordeum murinum'' ssp. ''{{Vanchor|glaucum}}''.<ref name="Mizianty-2006" /> Jakob & Blattner 2009 find it is [[diploid]].<ref name="Formation"/> It appears in warmer climates of the Mediterranean region.

The above subspecies differ primarily because of their chromosome numbers, spikelet morphology, and geographical distribution.<ref name="Mizianty-2006" /> ''H. leporinum'' is more dominant in areas where the rainfall is greater than {{cvt|425|mm|0}}.<ref name="Fleet-2012" /> ''H. glaucum'' is more dominant in semiarid regions where rainfall is less than that.<ref name="Fleet-2012" />

The last is the tetraploid ''Hordeum murinum'' ssp. ''{{Vanchor|murinum}}''.<ref name="Formation"/>

==Evolution==
Jakob & Blattner 2009 find the [[diploid]] subspecies [[#glaucum|''H. m.'' ssp. ''glaucum'']] is the only extant parent contributing to contemporary ''H. m.'' populations.<ref name="Formation"/> They find that another species of the same group – an extinct member of the {{Vanchor|Xu}} group – combined with it to form the [[tetraploid]]s, and another unknown extinct species then contributed to the [[hexaploid]]s.<ref name="Formation">

==Uses==
Although ''H. murinum'' is considered a difficult weed in cereal crop fields,<ref name="Fleet-2012" /> it is useful for feeding grazing animals.<ref name="Fleet-2012" /> It is also the main source of forage for cattle production in areas with water deficits.<ref name="Johnston-2009" />

==Cultural significance==
In England in the late 20th century among children the plant was referred to colloquially as the 'Flea Dart', from the aerodynamic shape of its seedhead, and the [[aphids]] that are often present within it in its immature state.<ref>'Wall Barely' entry in the 'Plant-Lore' website (2019). https://www.plant-lore.com/wall-barley/</ref> In China the subspecies ''leporinum'' is a common ingredient in the spring [[Qingming Festival]] snack ''[[qingtuan|qīngtuán]]''.
